content.page_title: Cardiovascular comorbidities — Arrhythmias and conduction disturbances
content.follow_up_timing: One follow-up visit recommended within 1–2 weeks after discharge.
follow_up_components: Monitoring of signs and symptoms of heart failure (HF)
Assessment of volume status, blood pressure, heart rate
Laboratory measurements including renal function and electrolytes
Assessment of iron status and hepatic function if not done before discharge
content.treatment_optimization_note: Based on clinical evaluation and laboratory exams, further optimization and/or initiation of disease-modifying treatment for HFrEF should occur.
content.evidence_note: Retrospective studies associate early follow-up with lower 30-day readmission rates; prospective randomized trials not yet performed.
content.section_12_overview: Cardiovascular comorbidities with subsection on arrhythmias and conduction disturbances.
content.atrial_fibrillation_summary: AF and HF frequently coexist and can cause or exacerbate each other via structural cardiac remodelling, activation of neurohormonal systems, and rate-related LV impairment. AF in chronic HF is associated with worse prognosis, including stroke and increased mortality.

recommendations_table_summary.recommendation: Evaluate patients hospitalized for HF to exclude persistent signs of congestion before discharge and optimize oral treatment.
Administer evidence-based oral medical treatment before discharge.
Early follow-up visit at 1–2 weeks after discharge to assess congestion, drug tolerance and start/up-titrate evidence-based therapy.
Consider ferric carboxymaltose for iron deficiency (serum ferritin <100 ng/mL or ferritin 100–299 ng/mL with TSAT <20%) to improve symptoms and reduce rehospitalizations.

key_terms_acronyms.HFrEF: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
